title: Child Poverty Is Down. And Yet So Are Reading Scores.
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman responds to a poverty researcher's claim that fixing reading problems requires addressing poverty and housing instability. He grants that poverty matters for reading outcomes and is a worthy goal in its own right, then points to the uncomfortable fact that child poverty has fallen significantly while reading scores have declined anyway. The Census Bureau reports the official child poverty rate fell to a historic low of 13.4 percent in 2025, down from 20.7 percent in 2009, and the supplemental measure tells a similar story. Using Michigan as a case study, child poverty fell from 22.6 to 18 percent between 2014 and 2024 while average NAEP scores dropped 8.3 points, and the whole performance curve shifted left across income and racial groups. Aldeman concludes that poverty cannot be the primary explanation for the literacy decline, and notes that Michigan's 2016 early literacy reforms produced modest gains, showing schools are not powerless.
points: Child poverty fell from 20.7 percent in 2009 to a historic low of 13.4 percent in 2025, yet national reading performance did not improve.
Michigan's child poverty rate fell from 22.6 to 18 percent between 2014 and 2024 while average reading scores fell 8.3 points.
The decline appears across income and racial subgroups, so it is not merely a subgroup problem.
Aldeman does not deny that poverty matters, only that it cannot be the main driver of the literacy crisis.
Michigan's early literacy reforms, with coaches, teacher training and support for struggling readers, produced modest gains, so schools can act without waiting for poverty to be eradicated.
quotes: There’s no question that poverty matters for reading outcomes. Children growing up in poverty may face housing instability or food insecurity, and they have less access to books or other educational resources.
But here’s an uncomfortable fact: Child poverty has fallen significantly over time, and yet reading scores have declined anyway.
By that measure, child poverty fell from 20.7% in 2009 to 13.4% in 2025.
But like the national numbers, Michigan has experienced a decline in child poverty. Between 2014 and 2024, the state's child poverty rate fell from 22.6% to 18%, according to Census Bureau data.
In Michigan, average scores fell 8.3 points from 2013 (in blue) to 2024 (in red).
Whatever is driving America's literacy problems, child poverty cannot be the primary explanation.
The gains were modest, but they provide evidence that better reading policies can make a difference.
But children who are struggling to read today can’t afford to wait for policymakers to fully eradicate poverty before tackling reading.
